statement: The function returns a result r and all of the following hold. Let freq(nums, v) be the number of indices j with 0 <= j < len(nums) and nums[j] = v. (a) len(r) = k. (b) For all i, j with 0 <= i < j < len(r), r[i] != r[j]. (c) For every i with 0 <= i < len(r) there is j with 0 <= j < len(nums) and nums[j] = r[i]. (d) For every entry x of r and every value y occurring in nums that is not equal to any entry of r, freq(nums, y) <= freq(nums, x). Thus r is exactly a set of k distinct values of nums with largest frequencies, in any order.
preconditions: 1 <= len(nums) <= 100000; for every index i with 0 <= i < len(nums), -10000 <= nums[i] <= 10000; 1 <= k <= the number of distinct values occurring in nums (k interpreted as its mathematical integer value). The answer is unique: there is exactly one set S of k distinct values occurring in nums such that for every x in S and every y occurring in nums but not in S, freq(nums, x) >= freq(nums, y), where freq(nums, v) is the number of indices j with 0 <= j < len(nums) and nums[j] = v.

statement: Whenever the function returns a result r, let freq(nums, v) be the number of indices j with 0 <= j < len(nums) and nums[j] = v. Let F be the multiset of frequencies { freq(nums, v) | v occurs in nums }, with one occurrence per distinct value v. Then the multiset { freq(nums, r[i]) | 0 <= i < len(r) } equals the multiset consisting of the k largest elements of F, counting multiplicities.
preconditions: 1 <= len(nums) <= 100000; for every index i with 0 <= i < len(nums), -10000 <= nums[i] <= 10000; 1 <= k <= the number of distinct values occurring in nums (k interpreted as its mathematical integer value).

statement: Let freq(s, v) be the number of indices j with 0 <= j < len(s) and s[j] = v for a slice s. For every slice nums2 of 64-bit integers with len(nums2) = len(nums) and with freq(nums2, v) = freq(nums, v) for every 64-bit value v, whenever the function returns r on nums and r2 on nums2, the set of entries of r equals the set of entries of r2: for every value v, v equals some entry of r if and only if v equals some entry of r2.
preconditions: 1 <= len(nums) <= 100000; for every index i with 0 <= i < len(nums), -10000 <= nums[i] <= 10000; 1 <= k <= the number of distinct values occurring in nums (k interpreted as its mathematical integer value). The answer is unique: there is exactly one set S of k distinct values occurring in nums such that for every x in S and every y occurring in nums but not in S, freq(nums, x) >= freq(nums, y), where freq(nums, v) is the number of indices j with 0 <= j < len(nums) and nums[j] = v.
